Coloplast (COLO.B-DK) · investment memo · 23 November 2026

Coloplast: a high-quality, low-risk annuity at about a fair price, at the wrong point in its expectations cycle

Share price DKK 510.2 on 16 November 2026. Coloplast's fiscal year ends on 30 September, so FY27 is the year to September 2027.

#0

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Coloplast makes ostomy bags, catheters and related consumables for people with chronic conditions. It is the global number one in each core franchise, public payers reimburse its products, its patients rarely switch brand, and its revenue can be forecast to within about one percent. None of these strengths is in dispute, and none of them will move the shares.

Seven conclusions matter, in order of importance:

1

November's reset changed Coloplast's business model, not only its targets.

The EBIT margin is now a level that management chooses (about 25%), and reinvestment is the line that flexes. The new policy ends five years of margin erosion, so EBIT growth roughly doubles to about 6% a year. The same policy spends operating leverage before it reaches profit: 6% revenue growth buys 6% EBIT growth and no more.

2

Earnings arrive in two phases.

EPS grows about 1.4% a year across FY27 and FY28, then 7-8% a year from FY29. Reported EPS exaggerates the dip and the rebound (FY27 -3.4%, FY28 +6.5%), because FY26's currency gains turn into FY27 hedge losses and then drop out. Underlying EPS grows about 5% in FY27, about 4% in FY28 and 7-8% a year after that.

3

Over the next 6-12 months the skew in expectations is mildly negative, the opposite of the positive skew we look for.

FY27 guidance should be met, but its floor is today's run-rate, so a raise is unlikely. Consensus EPS sits 4%, 6% and 8% above the model for FY27, FY28 and FY29, and nearly all of the gap lies below EBIT. The likely pattern is: guidance met, EBIT estimates held, EPS estimates trimmed.

4

The coming EPS cuts are small, below the operating line and finite, and their dates are known.

The cuts start at the first-quarter report on 9 February 2027. By the half-year report in May 2027 the market will know whether the gross margin has stabilised and Kerecis has returned to growth. By November 2027 it will know the Medicare bidding prices. After that, I can identify nothing further missing from consensus, and the compounding years lie ahead. The case is therefore about sequence: the skew can turn positive during 2027, and the signposts are clear.

5

Fundamental risk is low; share-price risk sits in the multiple.

The likely range of FY27 EBIT is about ±2%. One turn of the P/E multiple is worth almost 6% of the share price, more than the whole likely range of FY27 EPS (±3.6%), and the multiple follows bond yields and the sector more than it follows Coloplast.

6

The stock is early in a turn, not in a broadening phase, so a fair multiple is about 20x, not the guideline's 33.88x.

The shares have risen 24% in six months while EPS estimates fell. The guideline's 33.88x comes from a decade in which Coloplast grew faster, expanded its margin and operated with near-zero interest rates.

7

The return, plainly stated.

Of the model's +101% return over 18 months, 77 points come from the multiple. At a multiple I can support, the same model gives about +16% over 18 months and about 12% a year over three years, weighted to the later years, with small downside. Three options sit outside the numbers: a delay to Medicare bidding, a disposal of two business units, and lower bond yields.

Five judgements move the value of the shares most over the next one to two years. Topic #9 sizes each one, with its arithmetic.

1Whether the margin holds at about 25%
2How Medicare bidding lands
3What happens below EBIT
4Whether growth compounds from FY29
5What multiple the market pays
In a sentence: Coloplast is a high-quality, low-risk annuity at about a fair price, at the wrong point in its expectations cycle. The business case is sound, the upgrade case is not there yet, and the dates on which the upgrade case can emerge are known.

#1

Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Key messageForces acting on volume help Coloplast and forces acting on price and cost hurt it, so the environment supports revenue but squeezes the margin by half a point to one point a year.

Evidence

  • Demand. About 76% of revenue is Chronic Care (ostomy, continence, voice and respiratory care). Public payers reimburse more than 90% of Chronic Care sales, and patients stay for 10 to 30 years on the brand chosen for them in hospital. The underlying markets grow 5-6% a year in value. Organic growth excluding China was 7% in the fourth quarter of FY26. Demand did not weaken in 2020 or during the inflation of 2022-23.
  • Weak pockets. Two weak pockets each account for about 4% of revenue. In China, patients who pay for ostomy products themselves are trading down to local brands that sell for about 70% less, and management now guides China flat. In the United States, Medicare's flat payment rate for outpatient skin substitutes, introduced in January 2026 and kept for 2027, hit Kerecis, whose sales fell 12% in the fourth quarter; Kerecis's comparison base eases from the second quarter of FY27. A third pocket, wound dressings (about 9% of revenue), is flat because European health budgets are tighter.
  • Payers in Europe. From January 2027 Germany applies a general 3% reimbursement cut, and France proposes a levy on reimbursed devices (the French parliament rejected the draft budget, so the levy is not final). Germany and France together are 20% of revenue. If distributors absorb roughly half of the cost, as they did in 2014 and 2019, the two measures cost Coloplast about 0.3 points of FY27 growth.
  • Payers in the United States. Medicare competitive bidding for ostomy and urological supplies starts on 1 January 2028. About 6% of group sales are exposed: 5% through distributors and 1% through Comfort Medical, Coloplast's own retailer. Bidders register from 1 December 2026 and bid from 5 January to 10 March 2027, and Medicare publishes the new prices in late 2027. A bipartisan bill (H.R. 10787) would delay inclusion of these products to 2033; the bill is at an early stage.
  • Costs. Materials and freight costs rise 3-4% on about 55% of cost of goods sold (50-70bp of sales), and Hungarian wages rise at a high-single-digit rate from January 2027 (about 35bp of sales). Reimbursed prices are fixed, so Coloplast can pass on none of these increases.
  • Currency. Currency, a drag of about 80bp on the FY26 margin, becomes a guided tailwind of about 2% on FY27 revenue and up to 50bp on the FY27 margin.
  • One real accelerator. Since January 2026 US billing codes separate hydrophilic (coated) catheters from uncoated ones. Hydrophilic catheters are about 40% of the US market against over 90% in Europe, and they are already 76% of Coloplast's US catheter sales, so conversion pulls the US market towards what Coloplast sells.

Inference. External forces split cleanly by line of the profit and loss account. Every force that acts on volume is favourable or is fading as a problem. Every force that acts on price and cost is negative, moderate (half a point to one point of margin a year) and one-way, and it arrives in two dated steps: Europe in January 2027 and the United States in January 2028. The two sets of forces are moving in opposite directions: the demand pockets stop subtracting by mid-FY27, while price pressure is new and building.

So what. Organic growth of 5.5-6% is close to assured. External surprises will land on price and cost, and therefore on either the margin or the reinvestment that protects the margin. In FY27 the currency tailwind can absorb such surprises; in FY28 no such cushion exists.
Counter-case. The environment could turn out better. The delay bill, or a funding restriction attached to a year-end spending bill, has perhaps a one-in-four chance of postponing Medicare bidding. The French levy may not pass. Bernstein argues that the skin-substitute payment cap will clear out more than 100 high-priced competitors and let Kerecis's low-cost fish-skin products take share, though the numbers do not show that yet. The environment could also turn out worse. Private insurers and Medicare Advantage plans typically re-price off Medicare within one to two years, and bidding is designed to shrink more than 3,000 suppliers to about ten, which gives the surviving suppliers bargaining power in later rounds.
What would change my view. Progress of the delay bill in Congress; the final French budget; the published Medicare prices; Kerecis's hospital growth in the second quarter of FY27; freight and polymer prices.
Against the market. I agree with the market on the direction of these forces and differ on three weights. First, commentary gives the ramp-up of the Portuguese factory more attention than its size deserves (DKK 25-75m). Second, the market discusses Medicare bidding as an open-ended overhang, yet the plausible cost of bidding inside the forecast horizon is bounded (#9), and consensus FY28 growth of 6.1% probably leaves bidding out altogether. Third, the market barely discusses the second wave, in which private payers follow Medicare in FY29-FY30.
Conclusion: The environment gives Coloplast a top line that is very hard to slow and a margin that payers and costs squeeze by half a point to one point a year, so the environment meets this condition for revenue and does not meet it for profit.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Volume forces are favourable and structural (reimbursed chronic markets growing 5-6% a year, US hydrophilic coding pulling the market towards Coloplast, China and Kerecis drags fading by mid-FY27), but every price and cost force is negative, dated and building: the German 3% cut and French levy from January 2027, input and Hungarian wage inflation not passed on, Medicare bidding from January 2028 with private payers likely to follow, worth half a point to a point of margin a year. Consensus sales growth at the 70th percentile shows the volume leg; the net for profits is a slightly negative balance, in the 40s per the levels and close to the External change forces group (40), so it sits just below Kerry and above Carlsberg's mature, flat-volume environment.

#2

Corporate change

Key messageThe November 2026 reset is coherent and well funded but defensive: it stops the margin falling and does not lift earning power within two years.

Evidence

  • People. The top of the company has changed almost completely in 18 months. Gavin Wood became chief executive on 1 May 2026; he came from Johnson & Johnson MedTech, has a commercial background and has not previously been chief executive of a listed company. Niels B. Christiansen, chief executive of LEGO, is expected to become chair at the annual meeting in December 2026. The finance chief, in post since 2014, provides continuity, and he bought about DKK 5m of shares in March 2026.
  • Targets. On 2-3 November 2026 Coloplast reset its ambition to 2030: organic growth of 5-7% a year (from 7-8%); a flat EBIT margin in the "mid-20s" at constant exchange rates (CER), replacing the aim of EBIT growing at least as fast as revenue; and a return on invested capital of about 20% by FY29/30.
  • Resources. A savings programme called Funding the Journey frees DKK 500m a year by FY28, three-quarters of it in FY27. About 80% of the savings are reinvested in US Chronic Care, urology launches and R&D, and about 20% offset pressure on the gross margin. R&D spending rose 13% in FY26, and more than ten product launches are planned for FY27.
  • Repairs. Management has refocused Kerecis on hospitals (about 85% of Kerecis's sales), cut the Chinese organisation to size and ruled out large acquisitions. Capital spending falls from 5% towards 4% of sales by FY29/30, no new factory is needed before 2030, and Hungary's share of production volume falls from about 70% to 60-65%.
  • Unfinished. Five problems remain open. Turnover among US sales representatives has been unusually high since the reorganisations of 2025-26. The chief executive runs the Wound division himself for now. The Intibia nerve stimulator has slipped to FY27/28, and a rival Medtronic device is already cleared. R&D is still about 4% of sales, against 6-8% at medtech peers. And the fourth quarter of FY26, Mr Wood's first full quarter, clearly missed consensus, though against guidance he inherited.

Inference. The November reset is Coloplast's first coherent reset in five years, and its design is credible. The reset is also defensive by construction: it stops the erosion of market share, margin and credibility, and it does not lift earning power inside the forecast horizon. Its financial signature is a margin that stops falling, not earnings that accelerate. The reset rests on one capability Coloplast has never shown: slowing its own reinvestment when the gross margin disappoints. Between FY21 and FY26 Coloplast never cut selling spend when costs rose.

The Kerecis margin target is better founded than it looks. Kerecis's margin of about 1% in the fourth quarter of FY26 included DKK 30m of one-off costs on about DKK 290m of revenue, which is ten points of margin. Management's FY27 target of "above 10%" is therefore already close to the underlying run-rate, and reaching it is worth 30-40bp of group margin.

So what. For the next 18 months corporate change buys predictability, not upgrades. The real test of the reset is whether DKK 400m a year of reinvestment earns a return in Coloplast's share of new US patients, and 18 months is too short to see that return: each point of US ostomy share is worth only 0.10-0.15% of group revenue, and Coloplast took four years to win its last five points.

An option outside the numbers: a disposal. DNB Carnegie alone has raised a sale of the Women's Health and Kidney and Bladder Health units, for proceeds of DKK 4.5-6.0bn against about DKK 1.6bn of revenue and DKK 250m of EBIT. My arithmetic says such a sale is roughly neutral for EPS. Losing DKK 250m of EBIT costs 3.4% of FY28 pre-tax profit (DKK 7.4bn). Repaying DKK 5bn of debt at 3.5% saves DKK 175m of interest and gives back 2.4%; using the proceeds to buy back shares at today's price would instead retire 4.3% of the share count. DNB Carnegie adds that DKK 322m of overhead would have to leave with the units. The value of a sale therefore lies elsewhere: about half a turn less leverage, a simpler company, a route to the 20% return target, and the only path to a buyback before FY30.

Counter-case. The bullish reading is that a chief executive two weeks past a reset, with 45% of his annual bonus tied to each of the two guided measures, has built a base he will beat, as Convatec's chief executive did after 2019. The bearish reading is that too many senior roles changed at once, the US field force is unsettled just as Convatec attacks, and the first quarter on Mr Wood's watch was a miss.
What would change my view. A gross margin at or above 66% in both first-half quarters, with reinvestment intact. The award of the HealthTrust contract: Hollister's sole-source contract with this hospital buying group, which covers about 15% of US acute care, expired on 30 September 2026, and my sources do not report the outcome. A permanent head of Wound. Evidence that US sales-force turnover has settled. An announced disposal.
Against the market. The market's summary, "sensible reset, execution now key", is mine too. I differ in two places. First, I think the Kerecis margin target is safer than the sceptical consensus allows; Kerecis's growth is the unproven part. Second, where brokers debate whether the new targets are "beatable", I think the design of the reset answers the question: management reinvests any surplus, so a beat will appear as growth later, not as margin now.
Conclusion: Corporate change is real, coherent and well resourced, but it is defensive: it turns a falling margin into a flat one and does not, within two years, turn flat earnings into rising ones.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. A coherent, funded reset under an almost wholly new top team (DKK 500m a year freed, 80% reinvested in US chronic care, launches and R&D; Kerecis refocused, China cut, big deals off the table) is real, but it is defensive by design: it turns a falling margin into a flat one rather than lifting earning power within three years, it is not yet in the numbers, and it carries live internal problems (US sales-force turnover, no permanent head of Wound, Intibia slipped, a Q4 miss on the new CEO's watch). Richard's 'gently positive but mediocre' reading (CVS 55) fits a reset that lowered the growth ambition, so it sits just below Shell's delivered, incremental self-help and above Hexatronic, in line with the Internal change forces group (53).

#3

Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Key messageColoplast owns a top-quartile franchise in a rational oligopoly, but its moat protects volume rather than price, its returns have fallen to average, and its management is unproven.

Evidence

  • Structure. Ostomy care is a rational oligopoly: the top three suppliers hold over 75% of the market (Coloplast 35-40%, Hollister about 25%, Convatec about 16%). Coloplast also has 40-47% of continence care and about 85% of laryngectomy care. The profit sits with the manufacturer: a one-piece pouch reimbursed at about USD 2.88 at retail sells for about USD 2.16 wholesale and costs about USD 0.76 to make, while distributors earn operating margins of about 8%. New entrants have taken essentially no share of developed-market chronic care in five years.
  • Moat. The specialist nurse chooses the brand at hospital discharge, the patient then refuses to risk changing a seal that works, and service programmes hold retention near 100%. Coloplast's moat is wide in Europe. It is narrower in the United States, where Coloplast has about 20% of ostomy against Hollister's 40-50%, and where Coloplast's own retail arm has 5-10% of catheter distribution against 40% for Convatec's 180 Medical. The moat is weak in wound care, where Coloplast ranks fifth, and it is eroding in China.
  • Financial profile. The gross margin is about 66%. The EBIT margin was 25.7% in FY26 against 32.6% in FY21, level with Straumann and above the other close peers. Cash conversion runs at 80-90% of net income. Net debt is 2.4x EBITDA, with a BBB+ credit rating. Return on invested capital has fallen from above 45% in FY19 to about 16%, diluted by about DKK 25bn spent on the Atos Medical and Kerecis acquisitions; Coloplast wrote off a third of the Kerecis investment within three years.
  • The rival. Convatec targets 6-8% growth from 2027 at a 24-26% margin, raised its 2026 growth guidance on 18 November 2026, and launches Natura Body, a two-piece ostomy product, in the United States in mid-2027, aimed at the 60-65% of the US market that uses two-piece systems. Yet in the first half of 2026 Coloplast's ostomy and continence businesses grew 7% and 8%, against Convatec's 4.3% and 5.9%.
  • Management and owners. Management's five-year delivery record is poor (#4), and the team is new. The strategy's priorities are the right ones: defend the chronic core, attack the United States, fix wound care and spend more on innovation. The targets are realistic, do not stretch, and now sit below Convatec's. The culture is unfinished: engagement scores are good, yet former staff describe a drift to an "accounting-driven" culture, and Mr Wood has made culture one of his five priorities. The founding family and, since 1 October 2026, a foundation hold about two-thirds of the votes; their revealed preferences are a high and stable dividend, no buybacks and no sale of the company. Executives own almost no shares.

Inference. Coloplast is a top-quartile franchise inside an average compounding machine. Industry structure and the moat meet this condition in full. The financial profile meets it on margins and cash, but no longer on returns or growth. Management does not meet it yet: its goals do not stretch and its record is not a winning one, though its early actions are those of an operator who puts credibility first.

The moat buys durability, not price. Because the buyer is a public payer, clinical preference for Coloplast's products converts into volume and launch premiums, never into list-price increases. That limit explains how the best franchise in the industry is being caught on margin by its number-three competitor, Convatec.

So what. The moat puts a floor of 4-5% under organic growth even in a poor year, which keeps the fundamental downside small. The moat does not produce outsized growth, and Coloplast's valuation premium to Convatec has shrunk for fundamental reasons.
Counter-case. The moat's lag cuts both ways. New patients are a small fraction of the installed base, so hospital patient starts lost to Convatec today would show in revenue only in FY29-FY31; eighteen months of reassuring revenue are therefore not proof that the moat is intact. On the positive side, a chair who has run a family-controlled compounder (LEGO) and a chief executive whose strength is commercial are aimed squarely at the US gap.
What would change my view. Coloplast's share of newly discharged US patients (published only occasionally); Convatec's ostomy and continence growth against Coloplast's each half-year; the renewal of the Vizient hospital contract in June 2028; R&D moving above 4% of sales; executives buying shares.
Against the market. "Narrowing gaps" is the dominant narrative about Coloplast against its peers, and I agree with it for margins and group growth. I think the narrative under-weights the fact that Coloplast is still the faster grower in chronic care itself: the convergence so far is in wound care, infusion and margin, not in ostomy and continence share. I would not expect Coloplast's valuation premium to rebuild before FY29, nor to collapse unless Coloplast is losing US patient starts.
Conclusion: The franchise and industry structure are top-quartile and the financial profile is still above average, but the moat no longer converts into pricing or rising returns and the management team is unproven, so this condition is half met.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. Industry and moat are top-quartile (a rational ostomy and continence oligopoly with Coloplast number one, profit captured by the manufacturer, 10-30 year patient lock-in, revenue forecastable within about 1%), and margins are high (gross 65% at the 85th percentile, operating 27% at the 80th), but the moat protects volume and never price, returns on new capital are poor (about DKK 25bn on Atos and Kerecis, a third of Kerecis written off, ROIC from above 45% to about 16%; 10% at the 67th percentile), the margin has fallen 7 points in five years, and management is new on a poor record with targets that do not stretch. The high predictability holds it above Carlsberg's goodwill-diluted brewer, but two ordinary parts keep it below Tele2's clean oligopoly, coherent with the four groups (74, 62, 55, 45).

#4

Guidance: how conservative, and the record behind it

Key messageFY27 guidance is the most credible in five years and should be met, but it starts from the current run-rate, so a raise is unlikely and the record of delivery has still to be rebuilt.

Evidence

  • The record. Coloplast cut guidance or targets four times in the 14 months to November 2026. FY26 began with guidance of about 7% organic growth and about 7% EBIT growth at CER; the April cut lowered these to 5-6% and about 5%; the year delivered 6% and 4%. EBIT missed consensus in every quarter of FY26, by 1% to 8%. The previous strategy missed both of its targets (8-10% growth and a margin above 30%), and Kerecis delivered no growth and almost no margin against an acquisition case of 30% growth and a 20% margin. The misses share a pattern: in most years revenue landed within a point of guidance, while the margin and the lines below EBIT did not. The only upgrade in recent years was to one division's growth (Interventional Urology, in FY26).
  • Today's guidance. FY27 guidance is organic growth of 5-7%, reported growth of 7-9% and an EBIT margin of about 25% at CER, with a slow first quarter and a margin weighted to the second half. Management set the guidance about 55bp below pre-results consensus on growth and 60bp below on margin.
  • Where the floor sits. The bottom of the growth range, 5%, is the exit rate of the fourth quarter of FY26, and the margin guide of "about 25%" compares with 24.8% in that quarter. By contrast, when Convatec reset in 2019, its first guidance (2-3.5% growth and a 16-18% margin for 2020) sat well below its run-rate, and Convatec beat that guidance (4% and 18.5%).
  • The buffers. Two buffers protect FY27 guidance. Management can slow the reinvestment budget (1.3% of sales), and the "mid-20s" wording of the target leaves room for Medicare bidding, which does not affect FY27. Against these buffers, the gross margin has to average about 66.0% from an exit rate of 65.5%, while the cost and price steps arrive in January.
  • Steering the sell-side. Disclosure is much improved: management now gives cost building blocks, quarterly phasing, a pre-close briefing before each report and pre-announcements of large misses. Management has not, in my sources, guided financial items for FY27, which is where consensus is too high, and it will not quantify the effect of Medicare bidding or of "neutral to negative pricing".

Inference. FY27 guidance is credible and buffered enough to be met. It is not conservative enough to be raised, because its floor is the run-rate. My probabilities:

So what. The record tells the investor where to discount management's numbers: the margin and the lines below EBIT. The new framework tells the investor where that discount is now too harsh (the full-year margin, which management can protect with reinvestment) and where it is still due (the first-half margin, which reinvestment cannot rescue in time, and financial items). No guidance raise is likely in the next 6-12 months. The positive is that the guidance cuts have stopped.
Counter-case. The bullish camp (DNB Carnegie, Jefferies) calls FY27 guidance a beatable baseline: most of the savings land in FY27, and the Kerecis and China comparisons ease mechanically from the second quarter, so if the gross margin behaves, management has more room than it shows. The bearish point is that freight costs were already rising at double-digit rates in the fourth quarter, and Coloplast has never yet held a margin by cutting its own spending.
What would change my view. A first quarter no weaker than flagged; a first-half gross margin at or above 66%; guidance narrowed to the upper half of the range in August 2027.
Against the market. The sell-side is split between "beatable baseline" and "waiting for earnings growth to return" (Deutsche Bank, Morgan Stanley). I sit between the two camps and closer to the second: guidance met, not beaten.
Conclusion: Guidance is the most credible in five years and should be met, but its floor is the current run-rate and management does not steer estimates below EBIT, so Coloplast has still to build the record of delivery and upgrades that this condition asks for.

Score: 24, set by the Rater. Guidance or targets were cut four times in 14 months, EBIT missed consensus in every quarter of FY26 by 1-8%, the previous strategy's growth and margin targets and the Kerecis case were all missed, and the only recent upgrade was one division's growth; the new FY27 guidance is credible and buffered but its floor is the current run-rate, and management does not steer the lines below EBIT where consensus is too high. Disclosure has improved and revenue landed near guidance, so it sits above TT Electronics' restating over-promiser, but the two-to-three-year record is clearly worse than Indutrade's single miss, below the Guidance (45) and Sell-side estimates (40) groups because the brief weighs a recent record of misses heavily whatever the current tone.

#5

Business model: pricing power, leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Key messageColoplast has large operating leverage but spends it by policy, so 6% revenue growth produces about 6% EBIT growth and no more.

Evidence, lever by lever

Pricing power: none on like-for-like prices.

The model has price subtracting 0.3 points from growth in FY27, 0.8 in FY28, 0.5 in FY29 and 0.3-0.4 a year after that. Premium mix adds 1.2-1.3 points a year (convex and concave ostomy products carry premiums of 20-30%, the Luja catheter 5-10%). A price cut drops almost entirely through to EBIT, which makes price the largest single negative on the margin: about 30bp in FY27 and 50bp in FY28 before offsets.

Operating leverage: high, and spent.

Variable costs are about 22% of sales, so the short-run contribution margin is about three-quarters. The fixed cost base inflates 4-5% a year, which is why management says leverage "kicks in at around 5% organic growth"; above that rate the incremental margin is 35-45%. By policy, the surplus goes into selling costs (about 33% of sales) and R&D (4.0% of sales, rising to 4.4%).

Financial leverage: mild.

Interest is about 10% of EBIT, so a 1% change in EBIT moves pre-tax profit by about 1.1%. The real effect of the debt is to block capital returns, because the dividend takes the free cash flow.

Cost scope: real, and pre-committed.

The identifiable gross cost scope is 150-250bp of sales by FY30, from the savings programme, the manufacturing footprint, administration and the Kerecis margin. Only 30-50bp of that scope reaches EBIT, and it only offsets price cuts and wage inflation. Selling costs are the reserve that management could cut and has chosen not to.

Feedback loops: three reinforce, four balance.

Three loops reinforce growth: the installed base of patients compounds; US hospital access converts slowly into market share; and patients upgrade to premium products. Four loops balance it: payers cut prices as reimbursed spending rises; distributors consolidate; Convatec's own virtuous circle forces Coloplast to keep spending; and Coloplast's own hiring pushes up Hungarian wages. Convatec, by contrast, has mechanical margin tailwinds: USD 93m of amortisation rolling off, and general and administrative costs cut from about 13% to 6% of sales.

Inference. The loops sum to a revenue engine that is very hard to slow and a margin that is very hard to expand: Coloplast has to run to stand still on margin. Revenue growth of 6% produces EBIT growth of about 6%, and EPS growth of 7-8% only once the lines below EBIT stop subtracting. This condition, revenue growth leading to outsized profit growth, is not met, and the new policy is not designed to meet it.

What is new is that the leverage now works as a shock absorber in both directions. Between FY21 and FY26 the margin was the residual and absorbed every shock, with misses of up to 100bp. Under the new policy reinvestment is the residual, so the likely range of the full-year margin narrows to about ±40bp.

So what. Treat the unspent leverage and the cost reserve as downside protection. Using that protection has a cost that arrives later: reinvestment held back in the second half of FY27 shows up as slower growth in FY28-FY29. Selling costs as a share of sales are therefore the lead indicator to watch. If that ratio falls while the gross margin disappoints, management has bought the margin with future growth.
Counter-case. Three developments could let leverage through earlier. The R&D step-up could pay off sooner than Deutsche Bank's "not before FY30" and reopen launch premiums. Kerecis could go from no margin to well above 10%. And Coloplast could build a pricing function of the kind Convatec credits with 30-60bp of price a year, though there is no evidence of one yet. On the other side, if organic growth fell below 5%, leverage would work in reverse unless management cut reinvestment.
What would change my view. Organic growth above 6.5% with selling costs flat or falling as a share of sales; a margin guide lifted above "about 25%"; evidence of a pricing function.
Against the market. Brokers agree there is no operating leverage in FY27 and split on what follows: Deutsche Bank sees two years of margin decline, Morgan Stanley a flat margin, and DNB Carnegie and Jefferies gradual expansion. The model has the margin flat to slightly down in FY28, then rising about 20bp a year. Where I differ is on the discount for the record: the market still applies the rule that "Coloplast's margins always miss", and I think the risk has moved from the full-year margin to growth a year later.
Conclusion: The levers exist but are deliberately spent or blocked: price is negative, operating leverage is reinvested and the dividend absorbs the cash, so revenue growth produces equal profit growth and nothing more.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Structurally the operating gearing is large (variable costs about 22% of sales, incremental margin 35-45% above about 5% growth), but it is spent by policy into selling and R&D with the margin fixed at about 25%, the fixed base itself inflates 4-5% a year, like-for-like price is negative every year against public payers, financial leverage is mild and the dividend absorbs the cash, and balancing loops (payer cuts, distributor consolidation, Convatec) offset the reinforcing ones. The model's EPS grows about 5% a year against revenue about 6% (well below the median company's two times), so despite Richard's point that a high fixed-cost share is real leverage, gearing with no pricing power that is deliberately not converted sits a little below the ordinary 50, between the Economic strength (55) and Financial forecasts (35) groups.

EBIT is after amortisation of acquired intangibles. The end notes explain the basis of the last two rows.

EPS grows in two phases. FY27 and FY28 are years of digestion: EBIT grows about 5% a year and EPS only 1.4% a year. FY29 to FY31 are years of compounding: EPS grows 7-8% a year as the Medicare bidding cut annualises, interest costs stabilise and the margin edges up 20bp a year.

FY27 EPS falls while EBIT grows 6%, because of the hedge book, tax and refinancing. From FY26 EPS of DKK 24.70, EBIT growth adds DKK 1.51 a share, and financial items and tax together take away DKK 2.36, which leaves DKK 23.85.

Few analysts describe the hedging mechanism, so it deserves a careful statement. Coloplast sells its dollar and sterling receipts forward and books the result of those hedges in financial items, not in EBIT. When the dollar and sterling strengthen, EBIT therefore receives the whole currency benefit at once, and financial items give part of it back. FY26 was the mirror image: currency hurt EBIT, and financial items carried DKK 292m of currency and hedge gains. For FY27 the hedge book sits at DKK 632 per USD 100 and DKK 845 per GBP 100, against the spot rates of about DKK 668 and DKK 895 on which guidance is built, which implies hedge losses of DKK 130-175m if spot rates hold.

Two further items add to the FY27 drag: a normal tax rate (22.5%, after 20-21% in FY26) and, from May 2027, the refinancing of a EUR 850m bond that pays 2.25%.

Underneath, the EPS path is steadier. Excluding currency gains and hedge results from financial items, and holding the tax rate at 22.5%, EPS grows about 5% in FY27 and about 4% in FY28. The reported -3.4% and +6.5% are the same business seen through a hedge book.

Against the past: faster EBIT and EPS growth, slower revenue growth, no margin expansion

Growth a yearFY21 to FY26FY26 to FY31
Revenue8.3% (about 7% organic, plus acquisitions)6.1% (5.8% organic)
EBIT3.3%6.0%

  • Double-digit growth: in no line and in no year. The fastest growth is EPS at 7-8% a year from FY29.
  • Faster growth than the past: yes for EBIT; yes for EPS, but late; no for revenue.
  • Higher margins than the past: no. The improvement comes from the end of negative operating leverage; positive operating leverage has not begun.

Cash and balance sheet: the dividend absorbs nearly all free cash flow, and FY27 is tighter still. The dividend costs about DKK 5.2bn a year. In FY27 Coloplast also faces a cash tax payment in Iceland on the transfer of Kerecis's intellectual property, which DNB Carnegie estimates at about DKK 2.0bn against a booked charge of DKK 1.1bn and which is "payable in 2026/27". If Coloplast pays it within FY27, free cash flow covers a little over half the dividend, and net debt rises to about 2.5x EBITDA at September 2027, against the 2.3x that brokers show. Lower Danish tax over seven years recovers the payment, so its effect is one of timing. Leverage falls below 2.0x only in FY30, which leaves no room for a buyback before then, and return on invested capital reaches 18-19% against the target of about 20%.

Read FY27 EBIT as in line with consensus, and FY27 EPS as DKK 23.85 to 24.2. The upper end of that EPS range allows for two deliberately cautious model inputs, which I have left unchanged: a currency benefit of 30bp in the FY27 margin rather than the guided "up to 50bp" (worth up to 0.9% of EPS), and a tax rate half a point above guidance (worth 0.6% of EPS). The end notes give the reasoning.

So what. The forecasts describe a steady compounder that emerges in FY29. Until then they offer an investor who is seeking upgrades nothing but options.
Counter-case. Consensus's EPS path (+0.6%, +9.2% and +9.1% for FY27, FY28 and FY29) needs a margin of 25.4% throughout and financial costs falling to about DKK 610m in FY28, while debt is flat and the 2.25% bond is refinanced at 3.5-3.9%. The bull case for FY28 (EPS of DKK 26.8-27.2, which is where consensus sits) needs three things together: a bidding delay, a HealthTrust contract win and Kerecis back at double-digit growth. The bear case (organic growth of 4.5-5% and a margin of 24.3-24.7%) gives EPS of DKK 23.4 in FY27 and DKK 24.1 in FY28.
What would change my view. Company guidance for FY27 financial items; the timing of the Icelandic tax payment; the first-half gross margin; the coupon on the bond refinancing.
Against the market. On EBIT I am within 1% of consensus for FY27 and 2-3% below it for FY28-FY29. On EPS I am clearly below consensus (#7). The market calls FY27 "a flat year"; I expect a reported fall in EPS and an underlying rise.
Conclusion: The forecasts show mid-single-digit growth with no double-digit line anywhere: EBIT growth doubles to about 6% a year because the margin stops falling, but EPS grows only 1.4% a year to FY28 before compounding at 7-8%, so the improvement on the past is real, modest and late.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. 4.5% falls in the 0-5% band, so D; it is near the 15th percentile of the Universe's consensus EPS growth. I place it high in the band because the FY26 base is flattered by DKK 292m of currency and hedge gains (underlying EPS grows about 5% then 4% then 7-8%) and all growth is organic, but not at the top because the margin only holds at 25% against 32.6% in FY21, nothing reaches double digits, and the improvement is back-loaded to FY29-FY31.

The narrative. The sell-side has told the operating story in full since early November: a credible reset, a margin held by reinvestment, Convatec closing the gap, and Medicare bidding as the overhang. Four items are thinly told, and all four are negative: hedge losses, FY28 financial costs, the Icelandic cash tax payment, and private payers following Medicare. Two thinly told items are favourable: the disposal option and the Kerecis margin. I have little direct evidence on investors, as distinct from analysts. The indirect evidence is that the share price has run ahead of analysts and moved in step with the sector.

Inference. This condition is not met. For the next six months, expectations for EPS stand above the model. For months 6 to 18, expectations roughly match the model, with a binary policy event, the Medicare prices, at the end. Upgrades need outside help from a bidding delay or a markedly stronger dollar. My probabilities:

about 75%that FY27 consensus EPS is lower in six months
about 75%that FY28 consensus EPS is 3-6% lower by November 2027
about 15%for an upgrade cycle, which needs a bidding delay or a stronger dollar
about 1 in 5that FY27 EPS reaches today's consensus

Two features soften these downgrades. First, their quality: EBIT estimates hold within about 1% while EPS is trimmed below the operating line, which damages a valuation far less than the operating misses of FY25-FY26 did. Second, the downgrades are finite: once the hedge book has rolled over and Medicare bidding is in guidance, I can identify nothing further that consensus is missing.

So what: the sequence by which the skew turns positive

After the first two steps, consensus for FY27 is close to the model. The remaining asymmetry is then the bidding outcome, and once consensus carries the model's base case, that asymmetry is favourable: I put about 55% on an outcome better than the base (delayed or mild), 30% on the base and 15% on a worse outcome. That is the point at which this case could offer the positive skew it lacks today.

Counter-case. Upgrades could come sooner. A gross margin back at 66.5% by the half-year, with reinvestment unchanged, would show that the buffer is larger than I assume. If the company guides financial items near DKK -750m, most of my FY27 gap disappears and I am wrong by nearly three points. A stronger dollar lifts revenue and EBIT estimates at once, though it lifts EPS only partly because of the hedges.
What would change my view. Each development above is observable within 6-12 months. Investors can check the financial-items guidance and any movement on the delay bill at or before the report on 9 February 2027.
Against the market. This is where I differ most from the market. The market expects flat FY27 EPS and about 9% growth in each of FY28 and FY29. I expect a 3-4% fall in FY27, a rebound in FY28 that is largely optical, and growth of 7-8% from FY29 off a lower base.
Conclusion: Scope for upgrades in the next 6-12 months is low and scope for small, below-the-line downgrades is high, so this condition is not met today; the dates on which it can turn are May and November 2027.

Score: 27, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is about 70% likely to be held, 20% cut and only 10% raised, because its floor is the run-rate; consensus EPS is about 75% likely to be trimmed 1-4% for FY27 and 3-6% for FY28 (stale pre-results estimates still in the mean, hedge losses and financial costs not modelled), about -0.5 to -1.0 times the 6% revenue growth rate, well below the 40th percentile; the narrative is already told and its thinly told items are mostly negative. The cuts are small, below EBIT and finite, so it sits just below Indutrade's even odds and above Xvivo's larger, binary downside, consistent with The fourth set group (37) leaning further negative on guidance.

#8

Current momentum

Key messageThe share price has turned without the fundamentals: it rose 24% in six months, largely with the sector, while guidance, estimates and the narrative stayed weak.

Evidence

  • Price. The share price is 17.3% above its 200-day moving average, yet that average has not risen in any of the last twelve months. Relative strength is at the 58th percentile.
  • Estimates for FY27. Consensus FY27 EPS is down 4% over one month, 5% over three, 6% over six and 11% over twelve. FY27 EBITDA estimates are down 2%, 2%, 3% and 9% over the same periods. FY27 sales estimates are up 1%, 2% and 2% over one, three and six months (a currency effect) and down 1% over twelve months.
  • Ratings and targets. The share of buy ratings is falling, and the mean target price (DKK 483) is below the share price, although targets have risen 3-4%.
  • Guidance and narrative. Guidance was cut four times and then reset. The narrative has moved from "broken compounder" to "credible reset, show me".
  • Peers. The dashboard's estimate-revision scores are +14 for Straumann, +9 for Convatec and Demant, -3 for Coloplast, -12 for Alcon and -14 for Smith & Nephew. Convatec's shares rose 9% in a day on its guidance raise, while Smith & Nephew has just cut guidance again.
  • Sector. Makers of ostomy, continence and wound products rose 13.0% over the three months to 22 October 2026, after falling 14.4% over twelve months. Sixteen of the 22 stocks in the dashboard's sector carry the top valuation rating, so cheapness is a feature of the whole sector, not of Coloplast alone.

Inference. Price momentum has turned without earnings momentum. The two-year-forward P/E multiple rose from 13.0x in June to about 18.3x while FY27 EPS estimates fell 6%. A rising price against falling estimates, in step with the sector, is a move led by the sector and by sentiment, with an element of company-specific relief that the reset was not worse. Among peers, the momentum that matters most, Convatec's, points the other way.

So what. Three of the four kinds of momentum that this condition asks for are absent (guidance, estimates and narrative), and the fourth, price, has run ahead of them. That gap raises the sensitivity of the shares to the February report, when hedge losses first appear in the numbers.
Counter-case. Prices lead fundamentals at turning points. Morgan Stanley finds that European medtech stocks typically rebound through the multiple in the year after a major sell-off, and Convatec's shares returned 46% across 2019-20 while its EPS estimates were cut by about a fifth in each year. On that reading the price is correctly anticipating the trough, and the 200-day average will turn up within months.
What would change my view. The 200-day average rising; revisions flattening after the first-quarter report; the first upgrades to a buy rating; targets moving above the share price.
Against the market. There is little to dispute in the momentum readings themselves. I differ from the interpretation that the rise since May is a company-specific recovery: I attribute about two-thirds of the rise to the sector and to bond yields.
Conclusion: Momentum is weak on every measure except the six-month share price, which has risen with the sector while estimates fell, so this condition is not met.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. The two measures are mixed (C), but the parts strongly contradict the positive one: guidance was cut four times in 14 months and reset below pre-results consensus at the last results, FY27 EPS estimates are down 4%, 5% and 6% over one, three and six months, Buy ratings are at the 10th percentile and falling, and the 200-day average has not risen in a year, with only the six-month price (+24%, sector-led) positive; that moves the letter one step to D. I place it at the top of D because relative strength is positive, targets have edged up and the narrative has improved from 'broken' to 'show me', while Convatec's strong peer momentum cannot lift it.

Fragilities and requirements

  • One unproven mechanism carries the margin: reinvestment as the shock absorber. Management can slow reinvestment over a year but not within a quarter, so the first-half FY27 margin is still exposed.
  • The FY29-FY31 compounding needs strengths that Coloplast has not yet shown: hospital patient starts converting into community sales, a stable US field force, and launches that sell.
  • Adjusted EPS excludes special items that recur every year (about DKK 0.7 a share in FY27).

How sudden, how trackable, how material

  • Dated, trackable and bounded (the main risks): the gross margin, reported quarterly; the hedge and financial line, also quarterly; Medicare bidding, on the agency's published calendar; and European prices, with the January steps. The worst plausible bidding outcome inside the horizon costs about 3.5% of EBIT.
  • Sudden, low probability: a second Kerecis impairment (carrying value about DKK 6bn), which would hit reported EPS and credibility but not adjusted EPS; a recall or quality event (the urology recall of December 2024 cost DKK 70-85m, and transvaginal mesh litigation cost about DKK 6bn of provisions across 2014-20); a stoppage in Hungary (about 70% of production volume); and loss of a hospital buying-group contract (Vizient, up for renewal in June 2028).
  • Sentiment, whether or not fundamentals justify it: the share price sits above analysts' mean target after a 24% rise; a "dividend not covered" headline is possible in FY27 when the Icelandic tax is paid; Coloplast's shares are among the European stocks most inversely correlated with US ten-year yields, which reached 5.14% in November 2026; and money that rotated into defensive stocks can rotate out.
  • How many headwinds at once. In the summer of 2026 five families of headwind were active together: regulation, cost, currency, competition and China. Currency has since turned and China is guided flat. Regulation, cost and competition remain, and each now sits inside guidance.
  • How far to a trough. A fair trough multiple of 15-16x implies a share price about 15-20% below today's; a severe trough, at the 2026 low of about 13.5x, implies a price about 30% below today's.

Sector and cyclicality, with the precedents. Coloplast has no exposure to the economic cycle. The sector's cycles are driven by regulation and interest rates, and its precedents teach four lessons.

Counter-case. The case may be riskier than it looks, because its main risk is invisible. The risk work behind this memo named Coloplast a possible "false friend": apparent stability that masks decay, with R&D at about 4% of sales and a sales force losing experienced people. The installed base hides share loss for years. The lead indicators are Coloplast's share of newly discharged US patients and Convatec's chronic-care growth, not Coloplast's reported revenue.
What would change my view. Downward: a first-half margin below 24.5% with growth below 5%; Kerecis's hospital growth stalling; harsh Medicare prices with early signs of private payers following. Upward: two clean first-half quarterly reports; financial-items guidance near consensus; the delay bill advancing.
Against the market. The market's named risk is Medicare bidding. For the share price over the next 12 months I rank bidding third, behind the multiple (driven by bond yields and the sector) and the lines below EBIT. I think the slow risk, the loss of US patient starts, is the least priced because it cannot yet be seen.
Conclusion: The case is simple and its fundamental risks are bounded, dated and trackable, with a likely FY27 EBIT range of about ±2%; the larger risks are that EPS falls short below the operating line and that the multiple follows bond yields more than delivery.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. The case is simple and its fundamental range narrow: two guided numbers set EBIT, the FY27 EBIT cone is about +/-2% and the FY27 EPS cone 23.0-24.7 (+/-3.6%), drivers are dated and trackable, there is no economic cyclicality, and the worst plausible bidding outcome inside the horizon is about 3.5% of EBIT. It is held below MITIE by 2.4x leverage (69th percentile), noisier lines below EBIT with consensus above the top of the range, a regulatory binary in late 2027, an untested reinvestment shock-absorber, a hidden slow risk in US patient starts and a multiple driven by bond yields after a 24% run, but sits above OEM's broader uncertainty; above the Risks groups (57, 60) because the memo's quantified cones are among the narrowest seen.

#10

Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Key messageThe stock is turning up, early and unconfirmed, not broadening: the price and the multiple have turned, but earnings and the narrative have not, and the first confirmation comes in May 2027.

Evidence. The two-year-forward P/E multiple troughed at 13.0x in June 2026 and stood at 18.3x on 20 November. The share price is 37% above its June month-end level. Against that, the 200-day average has not yet turned up, estimates are still falling, one analyst in eight rates the shares a buy, and the guidance cuts ended only three weeks ago, with a floor that has not been tested. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the "Broadening" phase.

Inference. I read the phase differently: turning up, early and unconfirmed. The price and the multiple have turned; earnings and the narrative have not. A broadening thesis needs rising estimates and new buyers arriving for company-specific reasons, and neither is present.

The sequence from here follows the calendar in #7:

The turn can fail in two ways. If the next two quarterly reports disappoint, the stock returns to bottoming. If sector flows carry the multiple to 21-22x before earnings confirm the turn, the stock stalls, with the re-rating spent before the upgrades arrive.

So what. The lifecycle phase sets the fair multiple (#11) and the kind of return to expect. In an early turn, returns come from the absence of bad news, the roll forward of earnings and the dividend; upgrades come later.
Counter-case. The stock may already be broadening: the price is 17% above its 200-day average, targets are rising, and the reset removed the fear of worse news. Or the turn may be a false dawn: the rally is a sector rotation, the first quarter is flagged as slow, and EPS cuts lie ahead.
What would change my view. Estimate revisions turning positive; the 200-day average rising; the share of buy ratings rising.
Against the market. Brokers' Hold ratings imply "wait and see", which matches my reading. The dashboard's "Broadening" does not.
Conclusion: The stock is turning up in price but still bottoming in earnings: an early, unconfirmed turn, not a broadening thesis, with the first confirmation available in May 2027.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's 'turning up, early and unconfirmed' rather than the dashboard's Broadening or the computed Stalling: the price and multiple have turned (18.3x from 13.0x, 17% above the 200-day average) but the 200-day average is flat, estimates are still falling and will be trimmed again from February, only one analyst in eight rates a buy, and the first confirmation is the May 2027 half-year. An early turn with the cause for concern clearing is attractive in principle, but with the price running ahead of earnings and a risk of stalling if the re-rating is spent first, it sits just below Solid State's bottoming-to-turning and above Linea Directa's weaker-momentum bottoming.

#11

The fair multiple

Key messageA fair multiple is about 20x two-year-forward earnings, roughly where the shares trade; the guideline's 33.88x describes an older, faster-growing Coloplast in a world of near-zero interest rates.

The guideline. The guideline multiple is 33.88x two-year-forward earnings: the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history, which is the level the guideline assigns to a Broadening phase. That multiple is 85% above today's.

My view. The guideline's method is sound, but for this stock, now, its sample is wrong. I would not use 33.88x, for two reasons.

The phase is earlier (#10), and the guideline itself gives a turn a lower multiple than a phase of peak delivery.

The ten-year history describes a different company in a different interest-rate regime. In the dashboard's monthly series, from its start in November 2016 to May 2025, the multiple never fell below 21x; since June 2025 it has never been above 21x. Between the two periods, growth stepped down from 7-8% to 5-7%, the margin from a peak of 33% to a flat 25%, and the return on invested capital from above 40% to about 16%, while the US ten-year yield moved to about 5%. The ten-year range (10th percentile 20.9x, median 28.0x) was earned by a business that expanded its margin for a decade at near-zero interest rates. In 2010-12, with bond yields comparable to today's, the shares traded on 20-22x (DNB Carnegie).

What I would use. About 20x, in a range of 19-21x, applied to EPS as consensus states it. Four cross-checks point to that level.

  • The guideline's own rule, applied to the right sample. Over the 17 months since the multiple left its old range (June 2025 to October 2026, a span of 13.0x to 20.8x), the 80th percentile is about 20x.
  • Brokers. Brokers' target multiples run from 16x (Morgan Stanley, on FY28 EPS) through 18x (Bernstein) and 19x (Deutsche Bank) to about 24x at Jefferies' target price.
  • Peers. On the dashboard's measure Coloplast trades on 18.0x, between Demant and Straumann and far above Convatec, although consensus expects Convatec's EPS to grow 13-15% a year (table below).
  • First principles. A 4.5% dividend yield plus EPS growth of about 7% a year from FY29 gives a return of 11-12% a year at a constant multiple. With a ten-year bond yielding 5%, that return is adequate and no more, which says the current multiple is about right.
Reversion to normal is worth1-3 turnsof multiple (6-17%), not fifteen turns (77%). The old normal belonged to the old Coloplast.

Around the 20x centre, a fair trough is 15-16x, and 22-24x is reachable if two years of delivery coincide with lower bond yields.

One translation between bases is needed. The multiple's history is measured on consensus EPS, which is after amortisation of acquired intangibles, while the model's EPS is before that amortisation. So 20x on the consensus basis is about 19x on the model's basis, which is where the model shows the shares today (19.1x).

So what. With the shares at about a fair multiple, the return has to come from the roll forward of earnings and from the dividend, not from a re-rating. A re-rating to 22-24x is an option that needs both delivery and lower bond yields.
Counter-case. The multiple could be higher. Jefferies argues that 20x is appealing, a discount to European medtech, and that "Swiss clock" execution would restore the premium; Demant and Sonova returned to their ten-year average multiples in an unsupportive market, on product momentum. Eight quarters of delivery and bond yields 100bp lower could make 24-26x conceivable by FY29. The multiple could also be lower: Morgan Stanley's 16x rests on the view that Coloplast no longer earns its premium to Convatec, and the peer comparison above supports that argument.
What would change my view. Bond yields moving materially; organic growth back above 7% with a rising margin; the premium to Convatec stabilising as Coloplast's lead in chronic-care growth holds.
Against the market. The guideline is far above every broker. I am slightly above the brokers' middle (18-19x), because I give more credit to the lower fundamental risk after the reset and to the compounding from FY29.
Conclusion: My view is that the guideline's 33.88x belongs to a different phase and a different Coloplast, and that a fair two-year-forward multiple for an early turn in a 5-7% grower with a flat margin is about 20x, roughly where the shares trade.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Cheap on its own range and neutral against peers gives B. I place it at the floor because most of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year range was earned by a business growing 7-8% with a rising margin and ROIC above 40% at near-zero rates, and the memo's fair multiple of about 20x is only some 5-7% above today's 18.7-19.1x, so the shares are slightly cheap, not deeply.

#12

Total shareholder return

Key messageAt a multiple I can support, the return is about +16% over 18 months and about 12% a year over three years, not the model's +101%, three-quarters of which comes from multiple expansion.

The model's return at the guideline multiple (from the model's starting price of DKK 507.80 on 16 November 2026)

HorizonTotal returnA yearFrom earningsFrom the multipleFrom dividendsValue per share
18-month column, to 31 March 2028+101.4%+67.1%+11.1%+77.3%+4.5%DKK 1,023
Three-year column, to 30 September 2029+132.7%+34.3%+23.6%+77.3%+13.6%DKK 1,182

What drives each part of the return

  • Earnings (+11.1%, then +23.6%). This part is the roll forward of two-year-forward EPS on the model basis: DKK 26.6 today (FY28), DKK 29.5 at March 2028 (the average of FY29 and FY30) and DKK 32.8 at September 2029 (FY31). It is not growth in reported EPS, which falls in FY27. The weak years are already inside today's valuation window, and that is the most constructive feature of the return. The other side is that this part rests wholly on FY29-FY31 compounding at 7-8%, the lowest-confidence stretch of the forecast.
  • Dividends (+4.5%, then +13.6%). The dividend is DKK 23 a share each year. Confidence in it is high, because the controlling owners prefer the dividend to all other uses of cash, though free cash flow does not cover it in FY27.
  • The multiple (+77.3%). The model assumes the multiple rises from 19.1x to 33.88x by March 2028 and stays there. This part is three-quarters of the 18-month return, and it is the one assumption I do not hold (#11). A share price of DKK 1,000 was last seen in December 2021, on a multiple of 42x.

My reading. At my fair multiple, which on the model's basis is today's 19.1x, the return is about +16% over 18 months and +37% over three years, or about 12% a year: 7-8 points a year from the roll forward of earnings and 4.5 points from the dividend.

Two cautions apply. The first pushes the return later; the second could make it smaller.

  1. The first year's earnings roll is already spoken for. The market prices consensus EPS, on which the shares trade at 18.7x FY28 earnings, and the model's FY28 EPS is 6.4% lower. The "unchanged" row in the table therefore assumes that the market pays 20x the model's numbers as consensus falls to meet them. If the market instead holds 18.7x on a falling consensus, the return to March 2028 is about +9%, almost half of it dividend, and the return to September 2029 is about +30%. The convergence of consensus on the model absorbs roughly one year of earnings roll.
  2. The roll depends on FY29-FY31. If EPS grows 5% a year from FY28 instead of 7.6%, the three-year earnings part of the return falls from +23.6% to about +16% (#9).

The shape of the 18-month outcome, on multiples I can support. The return is about -2% at a fair trough multiple, +16% to +21% in the centre, and +32% to +44% on a re-rating to 22-24x. The earnings roll matters on the downside too: the same trough multiple, reached within months and before earnings have rolled forward, gives the 15-20% fall described in #9. The 18-month return is therefore skewed positively, with small downside, which is different from a positive skew in upgrades. The return is carried by the earnings roll and the dividend while expectations drift down, and it improves from the second half of 2027.

about -2%18-month return at a fair trough multiple of 16x
+16% to +21%18-month return in the centre, at 19-20x
+32% to +44%18-month return on a re-rating to 22-24x
about +9%if the market holds 18.7x on a falling consensus

Options not in the numbers. A Medicare bidding delay (about +2% to FY28 EPS, and removal of the overhang); a disposal (better leverage and focus, not higher EPS); and bond yields 100bp lower (a higher sector multiple).

Counter-case. For the guideline's return to be right, Coloplast would need to be back in its old regime by early 2028: growth above 7%, a rising margin and much lower bond yields. For the return to be worse than my range, the multiple would need to revisit 13-14x on cuts to EPS, which would mean the floor set in November had failed.
What would change my view. The same developments as for #11, plus evidence on FY29-FY31 compounding: Coloplast's share of new US patients and the outcome of the HealthTrust and Vizient contracts.
Against the market. Analysts' mean target implies a fall of about 5%. I expect a better outcome, because analysts' targets apply a static multiple to one year's EPS and give little weight to the roll forward of earnings and to the dividend, which together are worth about 12% a year.
Conclusion: The model's +101% over 18 months is 77 points of multiple, 11 points of earnings roll and 4.5 points of dividend; at a multiple I can support, the same model gives about +16% over 18 months and about 12% a year over three years, weighted to the later years and with small downside.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. About +15-16% falls in the 10-20% band, so C, mapping to about 62; I place it slightly lower because the first year's roll is spoken for (if the market holds 18.7x on a falling consensus the 18-month return is about +9%, half of it dividend) and the earnings part rests on FY29-FY31, though the distribution (-2% at a fair trough, +32-44% on a re-rating) has a modest lower tail and the three-year check is supportive.

#13

Summary conclusion

Coloplast is a top-quartile franchise that has just told the truth about itself. Its revenue is an annuity; its margin is now a chosen level defended by a reinvestment budget; and its cash goes to a dividend that its owners will not cut. The November 2026 reset ended five years of falling margins and repeated guidance cuts, and replaced the fear of worse news with a floor.

That floor has three consequences for an investor looking for a positive skew.

The fundamentals are low-risk and unexciting.

EBIT grows about 6% a year within a likely range of about ±2% for FY27. Nothing in price, operating leverage or capital allocation is set up to turn that into double-digit growth.

The next 6-12 months lean the wrong way on expectations.

Guidance is set to be met, not raised. Consensus EPS is 4-8% too high, almost all of the excess below EBIT, and analysts will trim it at dated events from 9 February 2027.

The return is respectable and comes late.

At about today's multiple the shares offer about 12% a year over three years from the roll forward of earnings and a 4.5% dividend, with about 15-20% downside to a fair trough multiple and one to three turns of multiple as upside. The guideline's 33.88x, and the +101% it produces, belong to a Coloplast that grew faster, on rising margins, with money nearly free.

What would give this case the positive skew we look for is specific and observable: the below-EBIT cuts passing through consensus; a gross margin at or above 66% and a return to growth at Kerecis at the half-year in May 2027; Medicare bidding quantified or delayed in the second half of 2027; and, as free options, a disposal or lower bond yields. Coloplast will be the same business on each of those dates. What will change is how much of the bad news is already in the numbers.

The four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 40, set by the Rater. The input forces roughly cancel and lean slightly negative (external 45: assured volume against building payer and cost pressure; internal 54: a funded but defensive reset), and the financial output is weak (EPS about 4.5% a year, D, with only 1.4% a year to FY28): the change stops the margin falling but does not raise earning power, so it is a mild net negative with profits growing well below the typical company, in the low 40s per the levels and consistent with the memo's D.

Foundations' Robustness: 72, set by the Rater. The value chain and industry are among the most robust in the Universe (concentrated oligopoly, non-discretionary reimbursed demand, decades-long patient lock-in, revenue forecastable within about 1%, high gross margin, BBB+), which on Richard's CVS reading carries a business with ordinary returns towards the 75 band; it is held below that by a moat that yields no pricing power, a margin that fell 7 points in five years, returns diluted by poor acquisitions, and a delivery record (topic 4 at 24) of four cuts in 14 months under a new, unproven team, so above the memo's C.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 63, set by the Rater. In substance it fits 'CfC Clearing in HQ low-cyclicality business on Q1/Q2 multiple, leading to reversion to normal': a high-quality, non-cyclical franchise on a multiple at the 1st percentile of its range with a credible reset; but today's problems blur the clearing (a Q4 miss, gross-margin pressure, Kerecis not yet growing, US sales-force turnover) and the business has changed so that the reversion leg's 'normal' no longer applies, an important element loose. Falling estimates and the price are timing, not counted here; between Richard's CVS 65-75 for clearing in a middling business and the 50s for a fit missing an element.

Case Riskiness: 73, set by the Rater. A boring case whose fundamental risks are mostly 'paper cuts' (EBIT cone about +/-2%, EPS +/-3.6%, a multiple low in its own range, risks dated and trackable), which on Richard's CVS reading sits in the high 70s; it is held lower by a management that does not yet steer the sell-side below EBIT and has a record of cuts, 2.4x leverage, a bounded regulatory binary in late 2027 and a share price that follows bond yields after a 24% run, coherent with topic 9 at 70 and the memo's B.

End notes

How to read the numbers

  • Forecasts are those of the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). I have changed no forecast input. "Viewforth" in the charts and tables denotes the model's forecasts.
  • EBIT is before special items, which is the company's adjusted measure and the one consensus uses.
  • EPS is on the consensus basis (before special items, after amortisation of acquired intangibles) unless marked "model basis". The model reports EPS before that amortisation, about DKK 1.1 a share (4%) higher. The return in #12 is on the model basis.
  • CER is constant exchange rates. Consensus is the FactSet median of 16 November 2026. Probabilities are my own judgements.
  • "Likely range" and "cone" both mean the range that covers about 70% of outcomes around the base case.
  • The hero shows the share price of DKK 510.2 on 16 November 2026; the return calculations in #12 start from the model's price of DKK 507.80 on the same date.
  • One check the files asked for: the "latest Earnings Review" in the research folder does cover the results for the year to September 2026, reported on 3 November 2026.

Notes to the forecasts (#6)

  • EBIT in the forecast table is the model's EBITA less about DKK 330m a year of acquired-intangible amortisation.
  • The last two rows of the forecast table (free cash flow and net debt to EBITDA) are the earlier Analyst's cross-check, which includes the Icelandic tax payment. The model's own cash flow does not yet carry that payment (an open note with the Financial Analyst), so the model shows net debt about DKK 1.5bn lower at September 2027.
  • The FY26 base for financial items: the components quoted from the annual report sum to DKK -403m, while earlier work in this file set used about DKK -480m. The difference changes how the DKK 2.36 FY27 EPS drag splits between financial items and tax, not its total.

Two model inputs left unchanged (#6, #7)

  1. The FY27 margin includes 30bp of currency benefit, not the guided "up to 50bp", on the reasoning that part of the currency flow is hedged. Hedge results are booked below EBIT, where the model now charges them, so this trim may count 10-20bp twice (DKK 30-60m, up to 0.9% of EPS). I have left the input unchanged because "up to" is a ceiling, the Hungarian forint works the other way, and the first-half gross margin is skewed down.
  2. The tax rate of 22.5% is deliberately half a point above guidance, which is worth 0.6% of EPS.

Note to the return (#12)

The earnings and multiple parts of the return multiply (1.111 x 1.773 is 1.970), and dividends are added. The horizons are the model's fixed columns, so they end on the dates shown.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. The percentile ("66th percentile") is the share of the stocks scored on that item that this stock beats. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
